nodes.description: Behavioural disturbance is the predominant presenting symptom, so often that most affected individuals are first assessed by psychiatrists.

evidence.reference_title: Prion disease resembling frontotemporal dementia and parkinsonism linked to chromosome 17.
evidence.snippet: Behavioral disturbances were the predominant presenting symptoms. Nine patients were first seen by psychiatrists. Eight patients manifested parkinsonian signs.

nodes.description: Cerebellar ataxia occurs but is a late feature; in the second reported (German) case cerebellar ataxia and EEG abnormalities were absent until the late stages of the disease, consistent with the cerebellar PrP deposition.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of glycosylation associated with the T183A mutation in human prion disease.
evidence.snippet: Additional neurological signs including cerebellar ataxia and EEG abnormalities were absent until late stages of the disease.

nodes.description: Global cerebral atrophy with hypometabolism is seen on neuroimaging, consistent with the widespread neuronal loss.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of glycosylation associated with the T183A mutation in human prion disease.
evidence.snippet: Clinically, this form of prion disease was characterized by early-onset dementia as the predominant sign, along with global cerebral atrophy and hypometabolism.

nodes.description: Early-onset (presenile) dementia is the predominant clinical sign, accompanied by global cerebral atrophy and hypometabolism on imaging.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of glycosylation associated with the T183A mutation in human prion disease.
evidence.snippet: Clinically, this form of prion disease was characterized by early-onset dementia as the predominant sign, along with global cerebral atrophy and hypometabolism.

nodes.description: T183A abolishes a hydrogen bond between Y162 (beta-strand S2) and T183 (alpha-helix H3) that, in the wild-type protein, is a gatekeeper interaction stabilizing the packing between the S1-H1-S2 and H2-H3 subdomains. Its loss produces the strongest native-state destabilization of any TSE-associated PrP variant - a melting-temperature drop of roughly 26-28 degrees C - and populates a misfolding-prone intermediate.
nodes.id: Destabilization of the PrP-C Native Fold

evidence.reference_title: Mechanism of misfolding of the human prion protein revealed by a pathological mutation.
evidence.snippet: Among these PrP variants, a mutation associated with very early-onset dementia and spongiform encephalopathy in patients, namely T183A (16), abolishes a crucial hydrogen bond between Y162 from the β-strand S2 and T183 from the α-helix H3.

evidence.reference_title: Mechanism of misfolding of the human prion protein revealed by a pathological mutation.
evidence.snippet: Under physiological conditions, this H-bond stabilizes the packing at the interface between the subdomains S1–H1–S2 and H2–H3 (SI Appendix, Fig. S1) (17), and its depletion by T183A induces the strongest destabilization of the PrPC structure among the TSE-associated PrP variants (18).

evidence.reference_title: Mechanism of misfolding of the human prion protein revealed by a pathological mutation.
evidence.snippet: Differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) revealed that T183A strongly destabilizes this huPrPC domain, resulting in a reduction of 28 °C in the melting temperature (Tm, Fig. 1A and SI Appendix, Table S1).

nodes.description: The destabilized T183A PrP has a strongly enhanced propensity to misfold and aggregate, forming amyloid under physiological conditions. Disease-associated protease resistance extends to non-mutated wild-type PrP recovered from patient brain, indicating recruitment of normal PrP into the self-propagating conformer.

evidence.reference_title: Mechanism of misfolding of the human prion protein revealed by a pathological mutation.
evidence.snippet: We show that the mutation significantly enhances the aggregation propensity of huPrP, such as to uniquely induce amyloid formation under physiological conditions by the sole C-terminal domain of the protein.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of glycosylation associated with the T183A mutation in human prion disease.
evidence.snippet: The additional appearance of a band representing diglycosylated PrPSc strongly suggests that non-mutated PrP also acquires protease resistance in the present setting.

nodes.description: The dementia is frontotemporal in type, with behavioural and personality change predominating; the overall clinical picture closely resembles frontotemporal dementia with parkinsonism (FTDP-17).

evidence.reference_title: Familial spongiform encephalopathy associated with a novel prion protein gene mutation.
evidence.snippet: Nine members of the family were affected by a dementia with frontotemporal clinical features, with a mean age at onset of 44.8 +/- 3.8 years and a mean duration of symptoms of 4.2 +/- 2.4 years.

evidence.reference_title: Prion disease resembling frontotemporal dementia and parkinsonism linked to chromosome 17.
evidence.snippet: These clinical features bear a considerable resemblance to those described in FTDP-17.

nodes.description: In cell culture the under-glycosylated T183A protein is retained intracellularly rather than trafficked normally to the cell surface, consistent with disrupted maturation of the mutant prion protein.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of glycosylation associated with the T183A mutation in human prion disease.
evidence.snippet: Cell culture experiments confirmed previous reports on intracellular retention of the mutant protein in vitro.

nodes.description: Codon 183 forms part of one of PrP's two N-glycosylation sequons, so T183A removes a consensus glycosylation site. The resulting mutant PrP is under-glycosylated, and the disease-associated protease-resistant PrP recovered from patient brain is predominantly the monoglycosylated form.
nodes.id: Loss of an N-Linked Glycosylation Site on PrP

evidence.reference_title: Loss of glycosylation associated with the T183A mutation in human prion disease.
evidence.snippet: This mutation results in the removal of one of the two consensus sites for glycosylation of PrP.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of glycosylation associated with the T183A mutation in human prion disease.
evidence.snippet: Western blot analysis of the patient's brain tissue showed protease K-resistant PrP with a definite preponderance of the monoglycosylated form.

nodes.description: A heterozygous threonine-to-alanine substitution at codon 183 is present from conception in every cell. It does not break the gene; it encodes a full-length but conformationally unfaithful PrP, and it does so through two distinct consequences - loss of an N-glycosylation sequon and loss of a fold-stabilizing hydrogen bond.

evidence.reference_title: Familial spongiform encephalopathy associated with a novel prion protein gene mutation.
evidence.snippet: A novel prion protein gene mutation causing a nonconservative substitution at codon 183 was identified in 2 neuropathologically confirmed affected individuals (mother and son).

nodes.description: Parkinsonian signs occur in most affected individuals (eight of twelve in the clinical series), reflecting the striatal (putaminal) involvement of the disease.

evidence.reference_title: Prion disease resembling frontotemporal dementia and parkinsonism linked to chromosome 17.
evidence.snippet: Behavioral disturbances were the predominant presenting symptoms. Nine patients were first seen by psychiatrists. Eight patients manifested parkinsonian signs.

nodes.description: The disease hallmark is severe spongiform change and neuronal loss concentrated in the deep neocortical layers, putamen and claustrum, with conspicuously minimal gliosis in the most severely affected areas and PrP immunoreactivity in the putamen and cerebellum. The striatal involvement is the anatomical correlate of the parkinsonism, and global cerebral atrophy is seen on imaging.

evidence.reference_title: Familial spongiform encephalopathy associated with a novel prion protein gene mutation.
evidence.snippet: Neuropathological examination of 3 patients showed severe spongiform change and neuronal loss in the deep cortical layers and in the putamen, but minimal gliosis in the most severely affected areas.

evidence.reference_title: Familial spongiform encephalopathy associated with a novel prion protein gene mutation.
evidence.snippet: The putamen and cerebellum, but not other areas of the affected brain, displayed prion protein immunoreactivity.
